newsitem.title: GERMANY: Giant steel takeover move adds to pressure on Kohl.
newsitem.headline: Giant steel takeover move adds to pressure on Kohl.

text.p: Plans for a mammoth takeover in Germany's steel sector look like piling yet more pressure on Chancellor Helmut Kohl at a time when his archetypally German consensus politics look more and more ineffective and fragile.

A week after coal miners marched on Bonn's government quarter to protest against subsidy cuts and job losses, Germany's steel workers were up in arms at the prospective takeover of steel giant Thyssen by rival Krupp.
The outcome would be a steel and engineering group with annual turnover of some 63 billion marks ($37.3 billion).

But the takeover would almost certainly mean thousands of job losses in the Ruhr valley coal-and-steel heartland, and underline how Germany has missed earlier opportunities to reform uncompetitive sectors.

But now that Germany has a post-war record 4.7 million jobless, Kohl is struggling to push through even limited tax and pensions reforms. The sense of crisis and an election looming in 1998 have made him resort to increasingly short-term answers.

"Bonn only seems able to tackle the problems of the past without focusing on equipping German industry for the future," said Klaus Loebbe of the Rhine-Westphalian economic research institute (RWI), based in Krupp's home town of Essen.

The miners managed to push Kohl into finding extra money to cushion looming job losses in their dying industry, and thousands of construction workers simultaneously prised out a 25 billion marks ($14.8 billion) investment programme after marching in Berlin.
The steelworkers clearly saw themselves in a similar light, taking up the "We are the people" chant used in the East German anti-communist uprising and again last week by the miners.
"This government is weak and has shown it can be put under pressure," said Bank Julius Baer economist Gerhard Grebe.
"The miners and the construction workers did it, I suppose if the steel workers march on Bonn they'll get some subsidy too," he added with mild irony.
For decades, Germany's coal and steel industries enjoyed subsidies that shielded them from competitive pressures, but also prevented them adapting faster to global markets.
Unfortunately for Kohl, those competitive pressures have now struck with a vengeance.

And now, every company that does manage to make itself leaner and meaner adds to the government's troubles by throwing its newly unemployed staff on the mercy of a generous welfare system -- just as Bonn is trying to slash spending to qualify for European economic and monetary union.
Kohl's discomfiture is meat and drink to the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), whose support Kohl needs for his big tax and pension reform plans, and who are content to see him squirm.
Last week the SPD -- which rules the coal-and-steel state of North Rhine-Westphalia -- boycotted tax talks with the government to ride the sympathy wave whipped up by the miners.

The early signs were that it would also line up behind the steelworkers to make life even tougher for Kohl, as North Rhine-Westphalia premier Johannes Rau said his state government would "certainly not approve of such a hostile takeover".

For many analysts, the German model of consensus between employers, workers and government which Kohl embodies has shown it is simply not flexible enough to cope with the rapid economic change of the 1980s and 1990s.

Kohl himself had no stomach to tackle difficult reforms during the upheaval of German unification in 1990 or the two brief recessions in 1993 and 1995, just as he shied away from a confrontation with miners last week.

Unfortunately for the veteran chancellor, the task of winning around Germans to face tough realities can only get more difficult. Perhaps the biggest challenge of all -- persuading them to accept a European single currency -- is only a year away. ($ = 1.690 German Marks)
